summaries.example: Imagine a seed growing into a plant. James might say the seed has a beginning ability that leans toward becoming a plant, while sunlight and water help the change happen. In a similar way, he thought powers of the soul lean toward seeing, thinking, and choosing when something awakens them.
summaries.summary: James of Viterbo was a Christian philosopher and theologian who lived in the late 1200s and early 1300s. He studied in Paris, taught theology, and later became an archbishop. His writings ask how philosophy and theology explain God, the world, and the human soul. James said theology should lead people toward love of God, not just information about God. He also explored God’s power, the ideas God has of creatures, and the way human abilities become acts of sensing, thinking, and choosing. A repeated feature of his work is his effort to find a careful middle path between rival theories. For example, he said relations are real, but they are not separate things in exactly the same way that physical objects are. He also held that the soul contains natural abilities that are ready to develop when helped by experiences and images.
key_ideas: James of Viterbo was a medieval Augustinian thinker who connected philosophy with Christian theology.
He said theology is meant not only to know about God but also to love God.
He distinguished what God has chosen to do from what God could do without contradiction.
He thought ideas of created things are present in God while still being distinct from God in a limited sense.
He believed the soul has built-in abilities that can grow into acts of sensing, thinking, and willing.
summaries.why_it_matters: James shows how thinkers in the Middle Ages used careful arguments to connect religious beliefs with questions about reality, knowledge, and freedom. His work also reminds us that a disagreement may not always have only two simple choices. A thinker may try to explain what is right in several positions and then build a more balanced view.

important_terms.definition: A person who studies big questions about God, knowledge, reality, and how people should live.
A power or ability that is ready to become fully active.
A real connection between things, such as being a parent or being equal to a number.
A special gift that, in James’s Christian view, helps people love God in a deeper way.

questions_to_think_about: Is knowing something the same as loving it?
Can an ability be present before we use it?
Why might someone try to find a middle position between two opposing views?
How could a connection between two things be real without being a separate object?

summaries.example: Consider the relation “being equal to.” Two numbers can really be equal, but equality is not a third object sitting beside them. James treats relations in a similar way: they belong to reality, yet they are modes of their foundations rather than fully independent things. This lets him avoid both saying that relations are merely inventions of the mind and saying that every relation is a separate substance.
summaries.summary: James of Viterbo was an Augustinian theologian active in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. His philosophical theology treats theology as chiefly practical: its fulfillment is not mere cognition but love of God. He distinguishes natural philosophy’s route toward God from sacred theology’s route, since grace makes possible a form of friendship with God that natural powers cannot achieve by themselves. In discussing divine power, James separates ordained power, which follows the order God has established, from absolute power, which extends to whatever is possible without contradiction. His account of divine ideas develops from an earlier position close to Aquinas toward a mature view in which ideas are both identical with God’s intellect and distinct from it as cognized objects. This limited distinction is intended to explain how God knows creatures without multiplying independent realities in God. Across his metaphysics and philosophy of nature, James repeatedly seeks intermediate positions. Being is analogical rather than univocal between God and creatures; relations are real but not independent things; and natural change involves both an intrinsic tendency and an external agent. His theory of cognition is especially distinctive: the soul contains innate, incomplete aptitudes for intelligible objects, which are activated by appropriate phantasms rather than produced through abstraction by a separate agent intellect. His accounts of freedom and political authority likewise combine self-motion or natural foundations with the action of other causes.
key_ideas: James makes theology principally practical because its end is love of God, especially the charitable friendship with God made possible by grace. Metaphysics considers God as the highest being, whereas theology considers being in relation to God.
His distinction between ordained and absolute power allows him to ask whether God can do things outside the ordinary created order, while still excluding contradictions.

James’s mature account of divine ideas holds that they are identical with God’s intellect in one respect but distinct cognized objects in another. Their distinction is limited and does not make them independent beings.

Being is said analogically of God and creatures: God is being through himself, while creatures have being through another. James also gives a qualified account of the distinction between essence and being.
Relations are real but have a weaker status than substances. They are modes of their foundations, not wholly separate things.

James’s theory of innate aptitudes rejects the need for a distinct agent intellect that abstracts intelligible forms from sense-images. Phantasms still help awaken intellectual aptitudes, but the intellect supplies much of the causal contribution.
summaries.why_it_matters: James is important because he offers a distinctive alternative within scholastic philosophy. He shows that medieval debates were not simply conflicts between faith and reason; they included detailed disagreements about causation, knowledge, divine unity, freedom, and political legitimacy. His preference for qualified distinctions and middle positions also reveals how philosophical systems can preserve parts of competing arguments while changing their meaning.

important_terms.definition: The medieval study of God and religious doctrine, using reason together with sacred teaching.
A science or inquiry concerned with action and its goal, rather than knowledge considered only for its own sake.
God’s power considered within the order God has established, including what God has willed according to wisdom.
God’s power considered more broadly: the ability to do whatever is possible and does not involve a contradiction.
A way in which something exists or is characterized without constituting a second independent essence or thing.
A natural, incomplete principle that inclines matter toward a form while an external natural cause helps bring about change.
James’s term for an innate readiness in a soul-power that can become a complete act when appropriately activated.
The view that some knowledge or conceptual content is present in the mind before it is acquired through ordinary learning.

questions_to_think_about: Does making theology practical change what counts as theological knowledge?
Can a distinction within God’s knowledge preserve divine unity, or does it threaten it?
What is gained by describing relations as real modes rather than independent things?
Does an innate aptitude explain learning better than an abstraction theory, or does it create new problems?
How can a will be free if it is influenced by objects and by the intellect?

summaries.example: Suppose you know how to play a new game but have not started playing. You have a readiness that can become an actual performance when the right situation begins. James compares some powers of the soul to this kind of readiness. The ability is not just empty, but it is not yet the completed activity either. An object, an image, or a change in a sense organ helps awaken it.
summaries.summary: James of Viterbo was a medieval Augustinian thinker who worked as a theologian and philosopher. He wrote about God, reality, nature, the soul, knowledge, ethics, and political authority. In his view, theology is not primarily an exercise in collecting information. Its main purpose is love of God. He distinguishes the way philosophers can move toward this love through natural reason from the way sacred theology, through grace, makes a deeper friendship with God possible. James also examines divine power. God’s ordained power concerns the order God has chosen, while absolute power concerns what God can do in principle, as long as it is not contradictory. His discussion of divine ideas tries to explain how God can know many creatures without becoming divided into many gods or parts. James says the ideas are one with God’s intellect in one respect but distinct objects of knowledge in another. In other areas, he tries to avoid extreme answers. Relations are real connections, but not separate things. Natural change comes from both a developing form already present in matter and an external agent. Similarly, the soul contains active and passive aptitudes that need stimulation to become actual acts of sensation or thought. These positions made James an original participant in debates with other late medieval thinkers.
key_ideas: James says theology is mainly practical because its goal is love of God, not only learning facts about God.
He separates God’s ordained power from absolute power and asks what God could do without contradiction.
He thinks divine ideas are in God in two ways: they are identical with God’s intellect, yet also distinct as things God knows.
James often looks for a middle position. Relations are real, but they are not separate things like substances.
He argues that natural change needs both a built-in tendency in matter and an outside natural cause.
He says the soul has natural aptitudes for sensing, understanding, and willing. These aptitudes become active when something stimulates them.
summaries.why_it_matters: James matters because he helps us see philosophy as a conversation in which thinkers test several possible answers. He did not simply choose one side in every debate. Instead, he often asked how each side had noticed something true and how the pieces might fit together. His views on knowledge, freedom, and divine power also raise questions that remain understandable today: where do ideas come from, what makes a choice free, and how should we describe different kinds of possibility?

important_terms.definition: The study of God and religious beliefs through organized reasoning, often in conversation with philosophy.
An ability or readiness that can develop into a complete activity.
A connection between things, such as being related as parent and child or being equal.
A way something exists or is arranged that is not a separate thing with its own independent essence.
The power to do what is possible and not self-contradictory, considered beyond the ordinary order God has established.
A natural beginning of a form in matter that works together with an outside cause during change.
A Christian gift that helps a person love God in a way natural human abilities cannot achieve alone.

questions_to_think_about: Why might James call theology practical even though it studies God?
What is the difference between something being impossible and something simply not belonging to the usual order of nature?
Can something be real without being an independent object?
Why would James need both an inner tendency and an outside cause to explain change?
If the will is influenced by the intellect, in what sense can it still be free?
